license: Independently authored; thresholds follow wp doctor defaults.

rules.title: Administrator with an unexpected email
rules.why: Attackers create administrators with support-style or look-alike addresses (Zimbabwe: support_admin@wordpress.com).
rules.remediation: Confirm who owns the account. If nobody does, remove it, then check for the mechanism that created it (triggers, cron, snippets).

rules.title: Hidden administrator capability
rules.why: Privileged grants under a non-site capability key or a legacy user_level can hide an administrator from the Users screen.
rules.remediation: Remove the foreign capability row after confirming it is not a migrated legitimate key; stale grants from an old prefix can simply be deleted.

rules.title: New administrator
rules.why: A new administrator since the last complete snapshot is the most common persistence step after a compromise.
rules.remediation: Confirm the new administrator with the team. Unexplained accounts should be removed and the site treated as compromised.

rules.title: Out-of-sequence registration date
rules.why: Backdated registration dates are used by trigger and SQL backdoors to make a new administrator look old.
rules.remediation: Compare with access logs; if the account is not known, remove it.

rules.title: Generic or attacker-style admin username
rules.why: Generic logins like admin or support_admin are common on attacker-created accounts.
rules.remediation: Rename or remove the account after confirming ownership.

rules.title: Application passwords on all accounts
rules.why: Checks metadata for every account, retaining no hashes. EWMS / Exotic CRM / Exotic-CRM Sync family keys require all recorded IPs to be trusted CRM hosts; deceptive names remain suspicious.
rules.remediation: Revoke application passwords that nobody can account for.

rules.title: Privileged open registration
rules.why: Open registration with a privileged default role lets anyone create an account that can change the site.
rules.remediation: Set the default role back to the normal member role or disable registration.

rules.title: Non-administrator role with site-control capabilities
rules.why: Roles other than administrator that can edit theme or plugin code, install plugins, manage users or options, or that grant the literal "administrator" capability are admin-equivalent for anyone holding them. Matching definitions are grouped across markets in Fleet triage.
rules.remediation: Remove code-editing and user-management capabilities from staff roles (Advanced Access Manager or the role editor) unless there is a documented need.

rules.title: Accounts on an email domain the network may not control
rules.why: Password-reset emails for these accounts go to that domain. A www-prefixed or one-letter-off copy of the site domain, or a placeholder domain owned by someone else, lets whoever controls it reset those passwords.
rules.remediation: Replace placeholder emails with addresses the owner controls, or a domain the network owns and receives mail for.

rules.title: Failed-login pressure
rules.why: Thousands of failed logins from hundreds of IPs in a week is credential stuffing. Read from the Activity Log plugin table when present.
rules.remediation: Confirm login rate limiting (Loginizer) is active, consider a WAF challenge on wp-login.php and xmlrpc.php, and force resets for targeted accounts.

rules.title: Bulk autoloaded secret options
rules.why: Hundreds of secret-named options (such as per-user login tokens) set to autoload are read into memory on every request and often outlive their users. Counted by name and size only; values are never read.
rules.remediation: Set them to not autoload and purge entries for users that no longer exist; ideally move tokens to user meta with expiry.

rules.title: Database trigger
rules.why: Triggers are used to re-create admins or block cleanup. Our escort_live_url_sync triggers are approved only by exact definition hash.
rules.remediation: Export the definition, drop the trigger if it is not ours, then check cron for a hook that re-creates it.

rules.title: Scheduled event or stored routine
rules.why: A clean WordPress schema has no events, procedures or functions; they can run SQL without WordPress.
rules.remediation: Export and drop the object after confirming nobody on the team created it.

rules.title: Active plugin not on the approved list
rules.why: An active plugin nobody installed is how crawl-page-optimizer appeared on Zimbabwe.
rules.remediation: Confirm who installed it. If nobody did, deactivate it, remove its files and check for other persistence.

rules.title: Suspicious plugin path
rules.why: Hidden or core-mimicking plugin paths are used to disguise malicious plugins. A root-level single-file plugin is valid WordPress and not suspicious alone.
rules.remediation: Inspect the plugin files on disk before removing.

rules.title: Plugin or theme changed
rules.why: Unexpected activation, deactivation or theme switches are early signs of tampering.
rules.remediation: Confirm the change with whoever manages the market.

rules.title: Unknown cron hook
rules.why: Reinfectors schedule cron hooks that rewrite injected content after cleanup.
rules.remediation: Identify the plugin that registers the hook; unknown hooks with code-like arguments should be removed together with their source.

rules.title: Cron volume
rules.why: More than 50 events or more than 10 copies of one hook (wp doctor thresholds) usually means a broken or abusive scheduler.
rules.remediation: Clear duplicate events and fix the plugin that schedules them.

rules.title: Malware-family option name
rules.why: Option names used by WP-VCD, Monit and similar families. Names can collide with legitimate software, so this is a review signal unless content corroborates.
rules.remediation: Inspect the option value; remove it if it is not owned by an installed plugin.

rules.title: Look-alike autoloaded option
rules.why: Payloads hide in large autoloaded options named like core internals.
rules.remediation: Confirm which plugin owns the option; add genuine names to the known-options list.

rules.title: PHP decode or execution function stored
rules.why: eval, base64_decode and similar functions stored as data are a review signal; the malware rules escalate when decoding reveals an executable sink.
rules.remediation: Inspect the value and its owner plugin.

rules.title: Unexpected serialized object
rules.why: Serialized objects of unknown classes can be used for object-injection gadgets.
rules.remediation: Identify the owning plugin; add reviewed class prefixes to the serialized-class allowlist.

rules.title: Active stored code
rules.why: WPCode, Code Snippets, header/footer options and builder custom code are favourite places to persist injected scripts.
rules.remediation: Review the snippet; remove anything the team does not recognise.

rules.title: Script or iframe in content
rules.why: Script tags, unapproved iframes and event handlers in posts, widgets and terms need review; malware rules escalate only with corroborating behaviour.
rules.remediation: Confirm the embed is intended; remove it otherwise.

rules.title: Unexpected writing system
rules.why: CJK, Cyrillic or Greek text on these markets is usually injected SEO spam. Foreign text alone is never a malware finding.
rules.remediation: Allow the script for this market if it is legitimate; otherwise remove the content.

rules.title: Spam vocabulary
rules.why: Pharma, casino, loans, Japanese keyword and Chinese escort-spam vocabulary are the signature of SEO spam injection.
rules.remediation: Remove the spam text; disable a list for a market only if the vocabulary is legitimate there.

rules.title: Hidden links
rules.why: Links hidden with CSS are a classic SEO-spam technique; screen-reader helpers are excluded.
rules.remediation: Remove the hidden block.

rules.title: Burst of published posts
rules.why: A day with far more published posts than the market's median usually means automated spam publishing.
rules.remediation: Review the posts published that day and remove spam; then find the account or API key used.

rules.title: Posts without an author
rules.why: Published content whose author no longer exists can be left behind by deleted attacker accounts.
rules.remediation: Reassign or remove the posts.

rules.title: Spam in SEO titles or descriptions
rules.why: Injected links or spam vocabulary in Yoast or Rank Math titles changes what Google shows for our pages.
rules.remediation: Edit the SEO title or description back.

rules.title: Redirect to an external domain
rules.why: Yoast redirects that send our paths to other domains leak traffic and rankings. Partner link swaps under partners/ are informational; other external redirects remain critical.
rules.remediation: Remove the redirect unless it is an intended partner link.

rules.title: New outbound domain
rules.why: New outbound domains in content since the previous complete sweep can indicate link injection.
rules.remediation: Confirm the link is intended; approve the domain for the market or remove the link.

rules.title: URL shortener links
rules.why: Shortened links hide their destination.
rules.remediation: Replace shortened links with direct ones.

rules.title: Approved comments with links
rules.why: Approved comments with links are a spam channel.
rules.remediation: Unapprove or delete spam comments and tighten moderation.

rules.title: Site URL mismatch
rules.why: siteurl or home pointing elsewhere hijacks every link and redirect on the site.
rules.remediation: Restore siteurl and home to the platform domain.

rules.title: Search engines blocked
rules.why: blog_public = 0 tells search engines not to index the market.
rules.remediation: Untick Settings → Reading → Discourage search engines.

rules.title: Admin email changed
rules.why: A changed site admin email redirects password resets and security notices.
rules.remediation: Confirm the change; restore the company address otherwise.

rules.title: Upload path changed
rules.why: A custom upload path can make uploads executable or serve them from elsewhere.
rules.remediation: Clear upload_path and upload_url_path unless intended.

rules.title: Permalink settings changed
rules.why: Permalink changes break every indexed URL.
rules.remediation: Restore the previous structure if the change was not planned.

rules.title: Autoload size
rules.why: Autoloaded options load on every request; above 900 KB they slow every page (wp doctor threshold). Runtime filters cannot be observed through the database.
rules.remediation: Set large rarely-used options to autoload off.

rules.title: Expired transients
rules.why: Many expired transients bloat the options table.
rules.remediation: Delete expired transients.

rules.title: Revision bloat
rules.why: Posts with many revisions bloat the posts table and can preserve old injected content.
rules.remediation: Limit revisions and clean old ones.

rules.title: Orphaned postmeta
rules.why: Metadata for deleted posts wastes space.
rules.remediation: Clean orphaned postmeta.

rules.title: Unexpected table
rules.why: Tables that are not core, known plugin tables or allowlisted, and parallel copies such as backupdb_*, need an owner.
rules.remediation: Identify the owner; drop abandoned copies after backup.

rules.title: Table integrity
rules.why: Tables without primary keys, MyISAM tables and mixed collations cause corruption and replication problems.
rules.remediation: Convert to InnoDB and add primary keys.

rules.title: Table growth
rules.why: Sharp table growth (by engine estimate) can reveal spam floods or logging loops.
rules.remediation: Inspect the table contents.

rules.title: Cron overdue
rules.why: Events overdue by more than 24 hours mean WP-Cron is not running, so scheduled expiry and cleanup stall.
rules.remediation: Check the server cron calling wp-cron.php.

rules.title: Action Scheduler backlog
rules.why: Failed or stale pending actions indicate background processing problems.
rules.remediation: Investigate the failing hook; purge old failed actions.

rules.title: Active plugin entry with no readable plugin, confirm on disk
rules.why: Signals supported by the October market database review.
rules.remediation: Confirm files on disk. Open wp-admin → Plugins to clear a dangling entry; if a hidden folder exists, inspect and remove it through the incident workflow. Database inventory cannot prove files exist.

rules.title: Activity Log compromise behaviour
rules.why: Correlates privileged actions, same-IP failures and reviewed campaign evidence. New IP alone is review-only. Approved staff installs and confirmed network addresses are informational; IOC evidence takes precedence.
rules.remediation: Review ownership and evidence before making any site changes.

rules.title: Privileged accounts use legacy MD5 passwords
rules.why: Signals supported by the October market database review. One finding per market contains the count and bounded account list.
rules.remediation: Review ownership and evidence before making any site changes.

rules.title: Stored integration secrets
rules.why: Known secret-bearing options expose integrations if dumps are shared. Values are never read.
rules.remediation: Rotate vendor credentials if a database dump was exposed.

rules.title: Banner exchange links or executable embeds
rules.why: Executable script or iframe on a published page is critical; plain links are informational business review.
rules.remediation: Confirm the exchange is an approved commercial relationship before removing it.

rules.title: Registration spam across all accounts
rules.why: Registration spam across all accounts. Counts and bounded metadata only; no message bodies or scam usernames stored.
rules.remediation: Review the evidence and follow the market incident or operational repair workflow.

rules.title: Campaign and rotating-IP account logins
rules.why: Detects IOC successes, rapid rotating-IP bursts, control sequences, or many distinct login IPs on a non-staff account with a suspicious key over the available 30-day window. Keyed-account rotation does not require an IOC-pool match.
rules.remediation: Review the evidence and follow the market incident or operational repair workflow.

rules.title: Email delivery failure rate
rules.why: Reports elevated failure rate over the latest 30-day activity window, or SMTP authentication errors even with a small sample. Includes failed/sent/authentication counts and sample size; no email bodies are stored.
rules.remediation: Review the evidence and follow the market incident or operational repair workflow.

rules.title: Accounts under campaign targeting
rules.why: Concentrated IOC-range failures against existing non-privileged accounts registered before the available 30-day window and with no successful login in it. Targeting is not compromise.
rules.remediation: Review the listed accounts before deciding whether to lock them; do not treat failed attempts as a successful takeover.

rules.title: Historical privileged-login alerts
rules.why: Parses only bounded Wordfence Admin Login alerts into username, IP, reported location and UTC alert-send timestamps. Bodies, recipients, headers and attachments are never persisted. Stored alerts are historical claims, not independently verified logins.
rules.remediation: Confirm the historical IPs with IT. Deleted actors remain visible. Use filesystem diagnostics separately; these alerts cannot establish file integrity.
